name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q01 - Population interactions and sign conventions

questiontext.text:
Match the interspecific population interactions with their respective outcomes for Species A and Species B (where \(+\) denotes beneficial, \(-\) denotes detrimental, and \(0\) denotes neutral interaction):

InteractionOutcome (Species A, Species B)
(a) Mutualism(i) \((+, 0)\)
(b) Competition(ii) \((+, +)\)
(c) Commensalism(iii) \((-, 0)\)
(d) Amensalism(iv) \((-, -)\)

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Interspecific interactions between populations of two different species are classified based on whether the interaction is beneficial (\(+\)), detrimental (\(-\)), or neutral (\(0\)) to each participating species.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Interaction
In mutualism, both interacting species derive benefits, giving the outcome \((+, +)\). In competition, both species suffer a loss in fitness, giving the outcome \((-, -)\). In commensalism, one species benefits while the other is neither harmed nor benefitted, giving the outcome \((+, 0)\). In amensalism, one species is harmed while the other remains unaffected, giving the outcome \((-, 0)\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each interaction to its outcome yields: Mutualism with \((+, +)\), Competition with \((-, -)\), Commensalism with \((+, 0)\), and Amensalism with \((-, 0)\), which corresponds to (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q02 - Suspension strategies for coping with stress

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms with the respective suspension or dormancy strategies they use to tide over stressful environmental conditions:

OrganismsStrategy
(a) Bears during winter(i) Thick-walled spores
(b) Snails and fish during summer(ii) Diapause
(c) Zooplankton in lakes and ponds(iii) Hibernation
(d) Bacteria and fungi(iv) Aestivation

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When stressful abiotic conditions are temporary and organisms cannot migrate, they survive by suspending metabolic activity or entering a state of dormancy to escape stress in time.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Organism and Strategy
Bears undergo winter sleep known as hibernation to avoid extreme cold. Certain snails and fish enter aestivation to avoid summer-related heat and desiccation. Under unfavourable conditions, many zooplankton species in lakes and ponds enter diapause, a stage of suspended development. Bacteria, fungi, and lower plants form thick-walled spores that germinate once a suitable environment returns.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each organism with its strategy gives: Bears during winter with Hibernation, Snails and fish during summer with Aestivation, Zooplankton with Diapause, and Bacteria and fungi with Thick-walled spores, which corresponds to (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q03 - Examples of commensalism mutualism and parasitism

questiontext.text:
Match the ecological associations with their correct descriptions:

AssociationDescription
(a) Orchid on a mango branch(i) Mutualism between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria
(b) Cuscuta on hedge plants(ii) Ectoparasitism with evolutionary loss of chlorophyll and leaves
(c) Lichens(iii) Commensalism where grazing host stirs up and flushes out insects
(d) Cattle egret and grazing cattle(iv) Commensalism where the epiphyte benefits while the tree is unaffected

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Close interspecific associations include mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected), and parasitism (one benefits at the host's expense).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Association
An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch benefits from support and light while the mango tree derives no apparent benefit or harm, representing commensalism. Cuscuta is an ectoparasitic plant on hedge plants that has lost its chlorophyll and leaves, deriving nutrition from the host. Lichens represent an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria. Cattle egrets forage close to grazing cattle because the cattle stir up insects from the vegetation, representing commensalism.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Orchid on a mango branch matches (iv), Cuscuta matches (ii), Lichens matches (i), and Cattle egret and grazing cattle matches (iii), giving (a)-(iv), (b)-(ii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q04 - Morphological physiological and behavioural adaptations

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms with their characteristic adaptations to extreme environments:

OrganismAdaptation
(a) Kangaroo rat(i) Thick layer of fat (blubber) below skin acting as insulator
(b) Opuntia(ii) Behavioural thermoregulation by basking in sun and moving to shade
(c) Polar seals(iii) Meeting water needs via internal fat oxidation and concentrating urine
(d) Desert lizards(iv) Leaves reduced to spines; photosynthesis taken over by flattened stems

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adaptations are morphological, physiological, or behavioural attributes that enable organisms to survive and reproduce in their habitats.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Organism
In North American deserts, the kangaroo rat meets all its water requirements through internal fat oxidation (producing water as a by-product) and concentrates its urine. In desert plants like Opuntia, leaves are reduced to spines to minimise transpiration and flattened stems carry out photosynthesis. Aquatic mammals like polar seals have a thick layer of fat (blubber) below their skin that acts as an insulator to reduce heat loss. Desert lizards lack physiological thermoregulation and maintain fairly constant body temperature behaviourally by basking in the sun or moving into shade.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each organism with its adaptation yields: Kangaroo rat with (iii), Opuntia with (iv), Polar seals with (i), and Desert lizards with (ii), giving (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q05 - Thermal and salinity tolerance classifications

questiontext.text:
Match the ecological terms with their correct definitions:

TermDefinition
(a) Eurythermal(i) Restricted to a narrow range of salinities
(b) Stenothermal(ii) Tolerant of and thriving in a wide range of temperatures
(c) Euryhaline(iii) Tolerant of a wide range of salinities
(d) Stenohaline(iv) Restricted to a narrow range of temperatures

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The prefix eury- denotes wide tolerance, whereas steno- denotes narrow tolerance; -thermal refers to temperature and -haline refers to salt concentration (salinity).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
Eurythermal organisms can tolerate and thrive in a wide range of temperatures. Stenothermal organisms are restricted to a narrow range of temperatures. Euryhaline organisms are tolerant of a wide range of salinities. Stenohaline organisms are restricted to a narrow range of salinities.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these definitions gives: Eurythermal with (ii), Stenothermal with (iv), Euryhaline with (iii), and Stenohaline with (i), corresponding to (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(iii), (d)-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q06 - Population growth equations and mathematical forms

questiontext.text:
Match the population growth concepts with their corresponding mathematical equations (where \(N\) is population density, \(t\) is time, \(r\) is intrinsic rate of natural increase, \(K\) is carrying capacity, \(B\) is natality, \(I\) is immigration, \(D\) is mortality, and \(E\) is emigration):

ConceptEquation
(a) Differential form of exponential growth(i) \(N_t = N_0 e^{rt}\)
(b) Integral form of exponential growth(ii) \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{K - N}{K}\right)\)
(c) Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth(iii) \(N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]\)
(d) Population density at time \(t + 1\)(iv) \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\)

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Population dynamics are modelled mathematically using discrete change equations for births, deaths, immigration, and emigration, as well as continuous differential and integral equations for exponential and logistic growth.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Equation
When resources are unlimited, the differential rate of exponential growth is \(\frac{dN}{dt} = (b - d)N = rN\). Integrating this equation gives the population density after time \(t\) as \(N_t = N_0 e^{rt}\). When resources are limited by carrying capacity \(K\), Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth is given by \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{K - N}{K}\right)\). Over a discrete interval from \(t\) to \(t+1\), population density changes according to \(N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each concept with its equation gives: Differential form of exponential growth with (iv), Integral form with (i), Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth with (ii), and Population density at \(t + 1\) with (iii), which is (a)-(iv), (b)-(i), (c)-(ii), (d)-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q07 - Ecologists and their contributions or principles

questiontext.text:
Match the ecologists with their landmark principles, experiments, or contributions:

EcologistContribution / Principle
(a) Connell(i) Resource partitioning among five warbler species on the same tree
(b) Gause(ii) Father of Ecology in India; founded postgraduate ecology teaching at BHU
(c) MacArthur(iii) Competitive Exclusion Principle under limiting resources
(d) Ramdeo Misra(iv) Field experiment on rocky sea coasts showing exclusion of Chthamalus by Balanus

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Key ecological principles of competition, co-existence, and ecological education are associated with specific scientists and their classic studies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Ecologist
Connell's field experiments on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland demonstrated that the larger barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller Chthamalus. Gause formulated the Competitive Exclusion Principle, stating that two closely related species competing for the same limiting resources cannot co-exist indefinitely. MacArthur showed that five closely related warbler species on the same tree avoid competition and co-exist via resource partitioning through behavioural differences in foraging. Ramdeo Misra is revered as the Father of Ecology in India and established ecology teaching and research at Banaras Hindu University.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each ecologist with their contribution yields: Connell with (iv), Gause with (iii), MacArthur with (i), and Ramdeo Misra with (ii), corresponding to (a)-(iv), (b)-(iii), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q08 - Life history variations and reproductive strategies

questiontext.text:
Match the life history reproductive traits with the organisms that exhibit them:

Reproductive TraitOrganisms
(a) Breed only once in their lifetime(i) Oysters and pelagic fishes
(b) Breed many times during their lifetime(ii) Pacific salmon fish and bamboo
(c) Produce a large number of small-sized offspring(iii) Most birds and mammals (repeated breeding)
(d) Produce a small number of large-sized offspring(iv) Birds and mammals (offspring size–number trade-off)

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Populations evolve life history traits to maximise their reproductive (Darwinian) fitness under the specific abiotic and biotic selection pressures of their habitat.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Trait
Pacific salmon fish and bamboo breed only once in their lifetime. Most birds and mammals breed many times during their lifetime. Oysters and pelagic fishes produce a large number of small-sized offspring. In contrast, birds and mammals produce a small number of large-sized offspring.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each reproductive trait with its example organisms yields: breeding once in a lifetime with (ii), breeding many times with (iii), producing a large number of small offspring with (i), and producing a small number of large offspring with (iv), corresponding to (a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH13_MCQ_Q09 - Ecological case studies in population interactions

questiontext.text:
Match the species with the specific ecological phenomenon they illustrate:

SpeciesEcological Phenomenon
(a) Prickly pear cactus in Australia(i) Predator maintaining species diversity by reducing prey competition
(b) Monarch butterfly(ii) Pollination via sexual deceit and pseudocopulation by male bee
(c) Starfish Pisaster(iii) Acquiring distasteful chemical during caterpillar stage from poisonous weed
(d) Mediterranean orchid Ophrys(iv) Invasive exotic species controlled by introducing a cactus-feeding moth

Choose the correct matching combination.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Predation, herbivory defences, and co-evolved mutualisms are illustrated by classic ecological case studies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s became invasive and was brought under control only after introducing a cactus-feeding moth predator. The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to bird predators because it acquires a special chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed. In the rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific Coast, the starfish Pisaster maintains species diversity by reducing interspecific competition among invertebrates. The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs sexual deceit, mimicking a female bee on one petal so that a male bee pseudocopulates with it and transfers pollen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each species with its ecological phenomenon yields: Prickly pear cactus with (iv), Monarch butterfly with (iii), Pisaster with (i), and Ophrys with (ii), which corresponds to (a)-(iv), (b)-(iii), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii).
